# Jung's *Aion* — Self, Christ/Antichrist, Fishes, Alchemy, and the Historical Shadow

## #0 — A psyche enters the history of its governing image

*Aion* begins with the person who says “I” and ends with a transformed relation to the psychic whole within which that person speaks. Between them Jung follows a Christian image of wholeness through its rejected contrary, its fish symbolism, its historical expectations and the alchemist's attempt to work what the governing image leaves unresolved. Each figure changes its office as the inquiry proceeds. The fish that signifies the redeemer will become food, monster, elusive substance and an attracting centre; the final return has to carry these encounters within it.

The source/production world of this whole is Jung's twentieth-century analytical psychology. His foreword is dated May 1950; the German work appeared in Zurich in 1951. He writes amid the European crisis of inherited religious orientation, approaching historical symbols through his experience as a physician. His narrated geography is much wider: Jewish and Christian materials of the eastern Mediterranean, Egyptian and Syrian cultic accounts, late-antique Gnostic texts, medieval European prophecy and heresiology, Arabic–Latin alchemical transmission, and the emergence of European natural science. These places are the settings and transmission routes of materials Jung interprets. They retain their differences within a book produced in a particular modern psychological world.

Three times operate together. The individual encounters autonomous psychic contents in a life; communities inherit and alter religious images across centuries; Jung arranges those historical materials through the symbolic time of the aeon and the precession of the equinoxes. He proposes meaningful correspondences among them. The existence of a source image, Jung's aeonic interpretation and the essay's subsequent use of historical frame-awareness each have their own standing.

The [Aion source house](../../../../episteme/sources/psychology/jung/jung-1978-aion-cw9-2/SOURCE.md) **sources** this telling, developed through selected passages of a recovered local Hull translation, a **1979 paperback reprint of the second edition whose copyright page records the additional 1978 corrections**. The house selects the 1978 hardcover printing; exact printing equivalence remains uncollated. Chapter, CW paragraph and printed-page locators below refer to the consulted carrier. They support paraphrase of Jung's argument; no quotation card has been promoted. The [whole-story law](../../../../../../../working/final-argument-quilt-2026-08-23/MYTHEME-WHOLE-STORY-AMPLIFICATION-LAW.md) **defines** the direction of reading: the complete interpretive movement precedes any reusable fish, Christ, Antichrist, alchemical or aeonic index.

## #1 — Ego, shadow and the image of perfection

The ego first appears as the centre of reference for conscious contents. Its rootedness in bodily and psychic conditions already exceeds what that centre knows of itself. Jung then brings the person up against the shadow: traits whose recognition requires moral effort because they belong to the person who repudiates them. Affect can seize the initiative. Projection makes an inwardly active factor seem to be a property conclusively encountered outside. The world then gives back the rejected face, while the resulting isolation appears to confirm that the world itself is hostile. The person can inhabit this self-reinforcing enclosure without recognising the activity that makes it. (Chs. I–II, §§1–5, 13–19; pp. 3–4, 8–10.)

The anima/animus movement deepens this problem of relation. In Jung's opening drama a son remains bound to an image of the mother as the giver of effortless fulfilment. Actual encounters disappoint the image; the demand that another person embody it prevents that person from being met. Differentiation requires recognising the image as a psychic reality and loosening its compulsory embodiment in a particular other. Jung's explicitly gendered anima/animus scheme belongs to his historical account; its extension to all persons is not assumed here. His dramatic presentation matters: the symbol acts through longing, loyalty, fear and attraction before the interpreter can make it an abstract object. (Ch. III, §§20–26; pp. 11–13.)

The approach to the Self consequently has a double danger. The ego can be overwhelmed by the larger psychic whole; it can also appropriate that whole as its own magnitude. Jung describes both directions of inflation and insists on discrimination, worldly adaptation and the relative autonomy of unconscious reality. A single formula cannot decide every conflict of duty. The integrating movement must leave someone capable of judgment and responsibility. (Ch. IV, §§43–49; pp. 23–26.)

Christ now enters as a culturally effective symbol of the Self. The image of the heavenly man, the second Adam and the restoration of the divine image gives wholeness a human face. Jung follows renewal, descent into the depths and the marriage imagery through which human life can participate in that image. Yet the perfection of the image produces a psychological difficulty: an exclusively good and luminous figure does not include all the opposites active in the psyche. In his argument with *privatio boni*, Jung keeps the experience and efficacy of evil in view even when its substantial existence is denied theologically. (Ch. V, §§70–77; pp. 37–42.)

Antichrist belongs to this ensuing drama. The contrary excluded from the representation of totality remains active and acquires a compensatory historical figure. The Christian aeon therefore bears an opposition within its own field of meaning: its dominant image and the counter-image answer one another. This is Jung's psychological interpretation of the God-image, with a distinct burden from Christian doctrinal judgment. Recognising an evil factor as real does not confer goodness on an evil act. The conclusion will return to the human suffering which a verbal reconciliation of good and evil leaves undiminished.

## #2 — The fishes give the age its temporal image

Jung opens the fish inquiry by noting that Christian interpretation gives Christ and the devil several shared animal symbols. A symbol can carry more than one valuation. The Christian fish has its own baptismal, eucharistic and epigraphic settings: the baptised live as little fishes, and the travelling believer of the Abercius inscription is fed a fish offered with bread and wine. Jung sets these alongside older Near Eastern fish traditions and then asks why the image became especially active around Christianity. He proposes astrology as a second source of its activation. The broad distribution of fish imagery and the specific Christian uses remain distinguishable within that proposal. (Ch. VI, §§127–128; pp. 72–74.)

Pisces lets the double figure acquire duration. Jung assembles planetary conjunctions, Jewish messianic calculations, medieval expectations and the precessional movement of the spring-point. His own notes sometimes correct the astronomy reported by his historical authorities. The calculations, their transmission and the expectations placed upon them are parts of his inquiry; an inherited forecast is not an independently confirmed causal law of history. The constellational image makes the contrary tendencies of an age visible together, while the age lives them successively. (Ch. VI, §§128–137; pp. 74–82.)

This doubled life also takes narrative form in Jung's report of the *Pistis Sophia*. A spirit resembling the child Jesus arrives at Mary's house and asks for his brother. Mary, uncertain whether it is a tempting phantom, binds it to a bed and goes to find Jesus and Joseph in the vineyard. On their return the double is released; the two embrace and become one. Jung interprets the meeting through a nature rising from below and a spirit descending from above. Here doubling leads to reunion. It cannot be given the same antagonistic office as Christ/Antichrist merely because two figures appear. (Ch. VI, §§131–133; pp. 78–81; Jung's mediated reading of that work.)

The historical pressure sharpens in the sixteenth-century turn. Jung reads the Church's schism and the outward movement of discovery and conquest of Nature as a crossing of the earlier upward religious aspiration. In his Nostradamus chapter, the letter to Henry II dated 27 June 1558 and the later horizon of revolutionary change make expectation itself a historical actor. Jung's reading places the Christian world's opponent within the European unconscious; projecting it entirely onto an external people would miss his psychological argument. His claims of precessional correspondence remain his interpretive chronology, including the difference between the sixteenth-century turn and the later dates named in prophecy. (Ch. VII, §§150–154; pp. 95–97.)

The subsequent historical fish chapter complicates any simple sequence of one deity replacing another. Jung considers the overlap of shepherd, ram and fish imagery around the beginning of the Christian era. In the account he takes from Epiphanius, worshippers at Alexandria bring a sacred image up from an underground sanctuary after a night of celebration, carry it around the precinct and return it below: the virgin has borne the Aeon. Jung explicitly notes that Epiphanius describes a pagan rite, while using it as testimony to Christian truth. Reception has already changed the image's argumentative office before Jung reads it. (Ch. VIII, §§162–165; pp. 103–104.)

The apocalyptic Lamb likewise refuses a single undifferentiated label. Jung contrasts the sacrificial lamb with the wrathful, many-horned conqueror. He calls the latter a shadow counterpart and distinguishes it from Antichrist. The shared scriptural field can contain a transformed Christ-image without making every darkening of that image the devil's son. His explanation invokes the historical resentment of Jewish Christians under Rome; that explanation is attributed to Jung rather than silently established as independent ancient history. (Ch. VIII, §§166–168; pp. 105–106.)

Ambivalence then becomes an action within the fish itself. In Jung's assemblage of Leviathan traditions, the monster opposed to God divides into a conflict between monsters; at the end the formidable creature becomes food for the devout. He relates this splitting to the differentiation and humanisation of previously undifferentiated psychic contents. Terror, opposition and nourishment are successive offices, not interchangeable dictionary meanings. His comparisons traverse distinct Jewish texts and their later receptions. The monster's conversion into a meal does not merge this source narrative with the project's independently authored Meal whole. (Ch. IX, §§181–187; pp. 118–121.)

## #3 — The fish is caught, worked and made to transform

Alchemy alters the position of the human participant. The image has become something to find and work upon, and the relation between the worker and the transforming substance becomes part of the transformation. Jung enters through the *Turba* tradition and its associated allegories, placing them within Arabic–Latin transmission. His historical dating and proposed routes belong to his scholarship and require separate controls for independent transmission claims. Within the text he reads, a round sea creature without bones or outer covering is heated slowly and treated with sea water until it shines; the preparation finally becomes an eyewash through which the practitioner can understand the art. The substance's alteration returns as an alteration in the capacity to see. (Ch. X, §§193–197; pp. 126–128.)

Jung's identification of this creature as a jellyfish is an interpretation of the recipe. He also records a sixteenth-century adept reading the round creature as an actual fish, and follows stones reputedly held within another fish's body. The opacity and radiance of the stone lead him through Saturn, lead and the bright mercurial substance concealed within darkness. The alchemical fish thus carries both the material with which the work begins and the transformed *lapis* toward which it proceeds. Its relation to the Christian redeemer is mediated through the *filius philosophorum*. The alchemical vocabulary does real work here: a hidden virtue is found within a difficult substance and becomes perceptible through an operation. (Ch. X, §§194–197, 213–216; pp. 127–128, 137–139.)

Jung also follows another, source-distinct pair of fishes through a revelation preserved in heresiological transmission from Carcassonne. John asks Christ about Satan before the fall. Descending through the elements, Satan finds two fishes yoked like oxen beneath the earth, working from west to east at the invisible Father's command. Fire halts his further descent; he returns upward, solicits the angels, falls, and receives a limited time in which to fashion the world. Jung then compares the fishes' ruling office with Augustine's priestly and royal interpretation of the feeding miracle. He expressly distinguishes that Christian pair from the heretical narrative and treats an identification with the elder and younger sons as conjectural. This preserves the story's agents, journey and limits instead of recoding its fish pair as a universal Christ/Antichrist cipher. His proposed Cathar–alchemical connection through Rupescissa remains a historical hypothesis. (Ch. X, §§225–229; pp. 145–147.)

The Echeneis brings the reversal into focus. In the received story this small fish can halt a ship despite its sails and rowers. Its attracting power overcomes the human intention to advance. But the alchemist seeks a magnet capable of attracting the fish itself and drawing the hidden substance to the surface. Jung emphasises this reversal: the practitioner now works with the power that previously held the vessel. The magnet can be taught; it names a doctrine or operative understanding as well as an instrument. *Mercurius* can consequently name substance and philosophy. The worker's changed relation to the elusive centre is integral to the work. (Ch. XI, §§239–241; pp. 154–156.)

Alchemy's aftermath changes the scale again. In Jung's account, the alchemical epoch gives birth to science in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and then recedes from view as an outlived mother. By the eighteenth-century division of faith and knowledge, each side has lost access to something the earlier practice tried to hold together. The investigating psyche itself disappears from the account of objective knowledge even while making that knowledge possible. This is the book's explicit route into scientific modernity: the child inherits an operation while forgetting the condition through which it became possible. The historical genealogy and Jung's account of psychology's relation to physics remain separately assessable. (Ch. XII, §§267–271; pp. 173–174.)

## #4 — The historical descent returns as a dynamic Self

The Gnostic return reaches back into the beginning of the era for earlier images of attraction and integration. Jung reads the Naassene teaching reported by Hippolytus as a water of doctrine that enables each nature to receive what belongs to it. He then distinguishes the Peratic serpent-Son who conveys signs down from the Father and carries their awakened substance back upward. In the first comparison doctrine attracts; in the second, the redeeming figure does. The distinction preserves the local movement within Jung's comparison. These are his readings of reported doctrines, not a replacement text for Hippolytus or a fusion with the separately housed Valentinian Sophia–Horos–Achamoth whole. (Ch. XIII, §§287–291; pp. 184–185.)

The question returns inward through Monoïmos: investigate the one who speaks of “my” spirit, understanding, soul and body, and the affects that arise without the ego's command. Jung compares this with Indian Self language while distinguishing that comparison from a demonstrated route of influence. The historical figures now lead back to the initial question of the ego's relation to what lives through it. (Ch. XIV, §§347–350; pp. 222–223.)

The concluding quaternio sequence makes the historical interpretation itself answerable. Jung explicitly acknowledges that his inserted **Shadow Quaternio** is a modern reconstruction absent from the Gnostic texts. He supplies the downward balancing movement because a purely upward orientation no longer describes the modern psychic situation. The disappointment of the expected return of Christ, increased human self-consciousness, the chthonic serpent and the approach to Nature form stages in that construction. His account of early natural science even distinguishes a crossing of the religious attitude from a simple reversal of it: the Paradise/lapis movement turns across that orientation. The broad aeonic opposition does not make every transition a 180-degree negation. (Ch. XIV, §§402–407; pp. 254–257.)

Jung then gives the sequence its own symbolic formula. The four major states are Anthropos **A**, Shadow **B**, Physis/serpent **C**, and lapis **D**; lower-case letters articulate the corresponding transformations within the states. The ring returns to its beginning through differentiation and integration. At printed p. 259 the connected diamonds show each whole unfolding into four and passing onward, rather than four unrelated emblems placed side by side. The return changes an unconscious totality into a conscious one. Jung describes a dynamic process within the Self and relates it to *solve et coagula* and the circular *opus*. His subsequent comparison with nuclear processes is explicitly hypothetical in §412. (Ch. XIV, §§408–421; pp. 257–265.)

This is the source-grounded place for the project's encounter with Jung's quaternary diamonds. His **A/B/C/D** schema has its own symbols and psychological assumptions. [Taylor's core theorem field](../../../../episteme/sources/internal-corpus/taylor/taylor-2026-core-theorems-pithy/SOURCE.md) **sources** the native **X/x** and all eight determinations, their sequence and inversions. The project can read the recurrent local wholes through its established recursive Bimba–Pratibimba operation only by preserving the particular whole unfolded at each stage: the Shadow's field is not the Anthropos field relabelled, and the resulting conscious return is not the unchanged starting condition. The [recursive Bimba–Pratibimba office](../../../../episteme/concepts/bimba-pratibimba.md) **defines** how an achieved field can ground its own internal determinations while remaining situated within a wider field. That operation is established in QL; the diagram-specific application here is **Offered; human-amplified: no**. It attributes neither the QL derivation nor a universal six-position scheme to Jung.

The conclusion returns to the clinician's first encounter with the shadow. It includes healthy instincts and creative capacities as well as morally reprehensible tendencies. The anima/animus figures also acquire positive and negative effects. The Self's *complexio oppositorum* requires this differentiated recognition; merely declaring all things good leaves suffering untouched. Jung turns attention back toward one's own error and responsibility. The history has altered what the person must be able to acknowledge, and the person must now live that changed relation. (Ch. XV, §§422–427; pp. 266–268.)

## #5→0 — The age becomes visible as an age

<a id="aion-historical-arbitration-return"></a>
The existing project operation is **historical de-monopolisation**. An age inherits a governing image; the image becomes an apparently immediate background of judgment; its exclusions remain active; contrary images and transforming practices expose the history within that background. An age can then become visible as an age, and its inherited measure can become revisable. This is the project-level return of the telling, distinguished from the independent historical verification of each genealogy Jung proposes.

This whole **compares** that movement with [A19's complex as local arbitration regime](../../../../episteme/arguments/A19-Complex-as-Local-Arbitration-Regime.md). Jung's projection passage supplies a specific psychological sequence of exclusion, apparent confirmation and isolation; the historical telling supplies the different sequence by which an inherited whole-image meets its contrary. A complex, a theological image, a Protected Account and a civilisation's symbolic frame have different substrates and evidential burdens. The return preserves their local powers while exposing an unwarranted claim to exhaust the containing field. The comparison was already authored; source precision develops its means of expression without downgrading its standing.

<a id="aion-differentiated-return"></a>
The whole **returns-to** [A21's individuation and recognition](../../../../episteme/arguments/A21-Individuation-Recognition.md) through the difference between returning unchanged and returning able to receive what previously could only be projected or excluded. The initial ego/Self distinction remains necessary at the end. The return into embodied judgment prevents a new universal name from becoming an enlarged persona. A21's **x→X→x** and **IS→AM** movements are authorial QL operations; this whole provides a named psychological-historical refraction after that derivation. The unresolved provenance of the phrase “becoming indivisible” is not settled by finding a related passage in *Aion*.

[Neumann's whole](../../../archetypal-ground/neumann-images/WHOLE.md) **compares** the shared archetypal ground: the round, differentiation from parental powers, heroic achievement and its transformation into a relation capable of receiving the transpersonal. Its [source house](../../../../episteme/sources/psychology/neumann/neumann-1954-origins-history-consciousness/SOURCE.md) **sources** that morphological account; Frank's sibling NOTES disclose his mappings and his encounter with Jung's diamonds, while copied excerpts remain uncollated leads. *Aion* develops a distinct world from this shared ground. Its particular historical image is Christian, its two-fish time is aeonic, its alchemical practice acquires a scientific aftermath, and its modern narrator explicitly reconstructs the shadow missing from the earlier configuration. Neumann's developmental morphology cannot supply the evidence for those geographical or historical details.

The success/succession seam likewise keeps two movements alive. **Generative succession** asks what further life or capacity a work makes possible. **Historical succession** asks how its achieved image becomes an inherited condition and later encounters its contrary or transformation. Alchemy's forgotten motherhood gives Jung's telling a concrete articulation of the latter. [Gebser's source](../../../../episteme/sources/phenomenology-continental-philosophy/gebser/gebser-1985-ever-present-origin/SOURCE.md) **qualifies** the comparison through the distinct relation of non-chronological Origin becoming transparent through historical consciousness. Jung's aeonic history and Gebser's Origin remain separate wholes; their conjunction is a project comparison, and the exact new symbolic appointment remains unratified.

<a id="aion-authored-register-boundary"></a>
Q27's subsection 6, “Aion, Job, and the Assumption — register decision,” supplies the already authored theological refraction that places Christ/Antichrist in the register of the **occupied slash**, after the native derivation. The Epi Paper's technoscientific reading adds the pressure of a tool that mirrors, distorts, amplifies or mediates a culture's spiritual and political constitution; its textual counterpart is representation appropriating the authority of living meaning. These are existing authorial operations, preserved as such. The exact assignments below remain separately unratified. The quilt's placement boundary also remains: Antichrist naming, Aquarian eschatology and a final showdown belong to the deep vault/tangential or plate register, not the manuscript's public historical proof. The Job–Assumption–Mother movement retains its separate whole. Neither a date for an Aquarian transition nor phenomenal subjectivity in an AI is established by this narrative.

--- title: "Māyā — Eye, Veil, Frame, Horizon" record_id: mytheme-maya-eye-veil-frame-horizon record_type: whole-mytheme register: mytheme claim_status: Argued source_relation: "Authored cross-source movement; historical witnesses separately qualified" human-amplified: yes --- # Māyā — Eye, Veil, Frame, Horizon This is Taylor's authored whole: an eye's constitutive blindside, Śakti's manifesting veil, a frame that claims the horizon, and recognition through the world that claim had enclosed. Its Śaiva, psychological, optical and technical passages retain their different sources. The declared amplification is human-amplified: yes; new symbolic appointments are human-amplified: no. The six turns develop this movement, including its dream, crystal, nested-relay and holographic subunits, without attributing their composite sequence to an inherited sacred narrative. ## #0 An eye opens upon a world. Something stands forward; something recedes. A face can be approached, a path followed, an obstacle avoided. There is a direction from which these things appear, even when attention belongs wholly to what appears. The eye's condition does not ordinarily arrive as one more face or obstacle. It is already at work in their appearing. Turn towards that condition. A mirror shows the eye, a diagram describes its structures, another observer supplies an angle unavailable from here. Each disclosure is real. Each also occurs through a further situation of seeing. The inquiry has not caught an accidentally overlooked object whose recovery would finish the field. Its own power of disclosure keeps exceeding the image it produces of that power. The blindside in this authored image is therefore more than the anatomical blind spot. It is the condition that lets a view have a foreground at all. A frame gives this condition an edge. Its exclusion is productive: a determinate appearance depends upon what it does not include. Without an aperture there is no particular photograph, without an orientation no particular prospect. The landscape under the conditions of aperture, frame and sensitivity is an actual appearance of the landscape. Its limits make this arrival possible. Taylor's [Draft 3 source](submission-package/essay/symbolon/episteme/sources/internal-corpus/taylor/taylor-2026-definition-god-draft3/SOURCE.md) **sources** that positive appointment of finitude. The whole begins with a capacity, before it meets the loss of relation that can overtake the capacity. The horizon differs from the frame. A frame bounds a presentation; the horizon concerns the field within which something can come forward, recede or be encountered at all. Walking changes what the horizon affords. Another person's reply changes what this situation asks. Neither movement requires the person to possess the whole in advance. Seeing already belongs to more than its current account. ## #1 The Śaiva passage gives this opening a genealogy. Anuttara/Paramaśiva names the unobjectifiable ground. Śakti is its power of manifestation and self-articulation: the appearing world is active disclosure. Prakāśa and vimarśa belong together as luminosity and reflexive awareness. The light is living; the power that displays also knows, distinguishes, joins and withdraws its displays. Māyā brings measure into this field. This appears, that is withheld; the subject and its object become distinguishable. The kañcukas give the bounded knower effective terms of life: kalā apportions what can be done, vidyā what can be known, rāga the desire of an incomplete situation, kāla its temporal limitation, niyati its determinate ordering. A person can act here, know this much, want something, wait, remember and stand in these relations. Paśu names the bounded position. Puruṣa and the inner instrument articulate an inhabitable field in which something is mine, something can be judged, and an intention can form. Buddhi determines; ahaṃkāra appropriates under I and mine; manas coordinates presentations and alternatives. Their activity gives experience continuity. A retained trace can be recalled; remembered material can be selected and recomposed into an imagined course. Memory is not already a command. The instrument can carry inheritance into a new act. The Śaiva account's universal subjectward and objectward orientations also precede the ego's local appropriation: the same words, “I am this,” have different scope when *this* is the whole manifest field and when it is a particular role or possession. [Dyczkowski's complete source house](submission-package/essay/symbolon/episteme/sources/indian-philosophy/dyczkowski/dyczkowski-2000-doctrine-vibration/SOURCE.md) **sources** the selected telling through its page-labelled transcript. Pages 65–68 develop the lattice and mirror; 69–75 develop reflexivity, memory, differentiation and return; 78–81 distinguish inner/outer manifestation and its activity. At p.79, creative separation makes a differentiated world effective. The veil belongs to manifestation's power. It is not an alien substance thrown across an otherwise finished spectator. The transcript remains source-matched, with selected-edition collation pending, and ends during p.81. The dream carries the same pressure intimately. A sleeper does not first construct a theory of sleeping and then choose to believe the dream. While dreaming, the fact of sleep can disappear from the experienced situation. Paths lead somewhere; encounters matter; fear and desire have an immediate world. The dream's objects need not be externally material to be objective within that experience. Waking changes their relation to their condition. It does not make the experienced urgency something that never occurred. Taylor's explicit sleeper correction supplies this subunit. In the later quilt, dissociation, tattvic contraction and the slash are appointed to the same event in the author's ontological register: a whole becomes locally inhabitable through difference whose condition can be forgotten. This is a substantive authorial identity claim. It neither turns the dream into empirical proof that the cosmos sleeps nor makes Kastrup's vocabulary and the Śaiva sources historically interchangeable. The proposed names Dreamcode and Dream-machine remain undeveloped naming proposals; the dream's operation needs neither as a new canonical entity. The crystal makes a different limit visible. A polished surface can display a landscape without knowing that display. Dyczkowski's p.70 contrast would leave luminous appearing unknown to anyone if reflexive awareness were absent. Adding another reflection to the crystal cannot by itself supply that missing office. The mirror here distinguishes the display from the awareness through which display is experienced; it does not establish machine phenomenality. In the Śaiva account the mirror of consciousness also generates and hosts its appearances: it does not need a second universe outside consciousness to deposit them. These two qualifications keep the living mirror from becoming an inert copying mechanism. ## #2 The second forgetting begins when a finite measure loses its relation to being finite. The frame now calls its own boundary the horizon of reality. What it cannot admit is redescribed as unreal, irrelevant or already explained. The operation that once made a situation intelligible becomes the authority by which every subsequent situation must be judged. This changes the eye's encounter with another person. Before the person can answer, the frame supplies a role, score, diagnosis or expected motive. Their words become further evidence of what the frame already knew. The account's success at arranging a world conceals the conditions under which it arranged it. A determination claims its determining power; `x` acts as `X`, the reflected image as its source, the local `1` as the `0` on which it depends. Constitutive limitation has become usurped jurisdiction. Psychically, a complex can make this arrest durable. An image attracts investment, investment colours what can be perceived, and the changed perception confirms the image. Its organisation is an achievement with a history, yet the organised basin now treats its own criterion as necessity. The forgotten field includes rejected alternatives, bodily and affective conditions, other agencies and other lives.
